Combray for researchers

Who holds the keys

How Combray protects your participants' data, from their browser to your analysis, and what that means for how you work. Participants get their own version of this story in the app, under Questions.

  • The participant's computer

    Holds their data, encrypted. It leaves only as a donation they choose.

  • The Combray server

    Run by the university. Holds keys and encrypted donations, but can read neither the data nor the donations.

  • The key page

    Unlocked with your passkey. Opens donations, in memory, while the participant allows it.

  • Data key. Encrypts a participant's local data. Never leaves their computer.

  • Small box. The wrapped data key, on the participant's computer.

  • Box key. Held by the server, released only for the participant's password.

  • Donation key. Fresh for every donation, covering only what was shared.

  • Sealed key. The donation key sealed to your public key, kept by the server.

  • Project key. Opens sealed keys. Kept locked for each researcher, under their passkey.

1

Participants' data is locked on their own computer

When a participant adds their data, the browser makes a data key that exists only on that computer, and encrypts everything with it. The data key goes into a small box (it is wrapped), which also stays on the computer.

The key to that box is held by the Combray server, which hands it out only for the participant's password. Neither the computer alone nor the server alone can open the data.

2

When they stop, the browser forgets

On closing the page, locking, or after 15 minutes without input, the browser throws away the keys and everything it decrypted. What remains on the disk is ciphertext and a closed box.

This is what makes shared lab computers safe: the next person at the computer cannot open anything without the password, and password guessing is limited by the server.

You never get the data key. It covers everything a participant loaded, including what they choose not to share.

3

A donation gets its own key, locked for you

When a participant donates, they choose exactly what to share. The browser makes a fresh donation key for that selection, and seals it to your project's public key: like a letterbox, anyone can put a key in, only your project key opens it.

The server stores the encrypted donation and the sealed key in separate places, and can open neither. The sealing uses a hybrid post-quantum construction (X-Wing), so recording the traffic today does not help an attacker with a future quantum computer.

4

Your tools borrow the key, every time

You open donations on the key page, a small page of its own that you unlock with your passkey (Face ID, a fingerprint, or your phone). Every time, it fetches the sealed keys from the server, opens them with the project key, decrypts in memory, and throws the keys away when it is done. Later the R package will work the same way.

The server keeps the project key only locked for each researcher, and your copy only locked under your passkey, so it cannot open anything itself. Nothing is installed on your computer, and nothing is left on it unless you save an export.

5

Withdrawal reaches every copy

When a participant withdraws, or asks you to withdraw for them, the server deletes the sealed keys and the envelope, and keeps a note that the donation was withdrawn. Your tool then deletes its local copy too. Any copy that is left, anywhere, can no longer be opened.

Backups of the server's key database could still hold a withdrawn key until they expire. The server's backup retention is a setting, 30 days by default, and participants are told that withdrawal is complete within that time.

Data you decrypt and save yourself is outside this protection. If you export a file, you are responsible for it under the GDPR, including deleting it when a participant withdraws.

6Coming later

Participants can take their locked data with them

Participants will be able to download a Combray package: their encrypted data and the closed box, in one file. It opens on any computer, but only after logging in with their password, and it stops working when they delete their data on the server.

Who can see what

Data on the participant's computerDonations
The participant, with their password●Yes●Yes, until withdrawn
Someone with the participant's computer○No○No
The server operator○Only with the participant's computer too○No
You, the researcher○No●Yes, until withdrawn or you are removed from the project
Someone with your email○No○No: they also need your passkey or recovery code

What this asks of you

  • Keep your recovery code safe, printed or saved apart from your passkey. If you lose both, a colleague can give you access again; if nobody on the project has access, nobody can open the donations.
  • Compare key codes when you give a colleague access, by phone or in person. It is what stops anyone slipping in a key of their own.
  • Analyse without saving. Write scripts that start from the encrypted donations and fetch the keys, rather than saving decrypted data.
  • In R, turn off "Save workspace on exit" (RStudio: Tools, Global Options, General, set it to Never). Otherwise .RData quietly keeps decrypted data.
  • Use a synced passkey (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, or a password manager), so losing a phone does not lock you out. Remove a lost device's passkey on the key page.
  • If you export data, you own that copy. Keep a list of exports, so you can delete a participant's data when they withdraw.

Analysing in R

The R package is planned. This is a sketch of how it will work; nothing is written to disk except the encrypted donations.

library(combray)

con <- combray_connect(
  server  = "https://combray.uni.nl",
  project = "willow",
  key     = combray_device_key()     # added once from the key page
)

combray_sync(con)                 # new donations in, withdrawn ones out
yt <- combray_read(con, dataset = "youtube_watch_history")  # decrypted in memory only
The full design, with every key, the constructions and the alternatives we rejected, is in key-design.md; how you sign in and hold your keys is in researcher-keys.md.
